newsitem.title: UK: Entrepreneur Goldsmith reopens British Euro battle.
newsitem.headline: Entrepreneur Goldsmith reopens British Euro battle.

text.p: Billionaire Sir James Goldsmith on Thursday called for British voters to be asked whether they want to stay in the European Union or to be part of a looser trading bloc, reopening a row which has split the ruling Conservatives.
He was immediately dismissed as "naive" by Sir Leon Brittan, vice-president of the European Commission.
Goldsmith made his call in a speech on Wednesday night to the Oxford University debating club.

He drove it home with full-page newspaper advertisements on Thursday, saying voters should be given a choice between staying in what he termed a federal Europe or returning to the "common market" bloc of the 1970s and early 1980s.
The adverts, in the name of his Referendum Party which he set up with his own money two years ago, set out for the first time the actual question Goldsmith wants put to voters.
"Do you want the U.K. to be part of a federal Europe or do you want the U.K. to return to an association of sovereign nations that are part of a common trading market," they asked.
Goldsmith's new party has attracted support from right-wing Conservative voters worried at Brussels' hold over British affairs and fearful of further integration.
But Brittan said Goldsmith was painting "a beguilingly simple" picture. "Unfortunately life is not that simple. The European single market is not just a row of barrows and stalls."

Without institutions like the European Court of Justice, the European Commission and the European Parliament -- which Goldsmith said in his advert amounted to a federal Europe -- a barrier-free market could not be held together, Brittan said.

"The option of a loose, non-binding European market with weak institutions is not on offer," Brittan said in a speech to the Cambridge University debating society due to be given on Thursday night but released early to the media.

"It would not work and pushing for it would be tantamount to asking for Britain's withdrawal from the European Union," he said, adding that voters would "resoundingly" reject any attempt to take Britain out of Europe.

Goldsmith's clarification of his demands sparked sharp reactions from leading Conservatives, who are trying to keep their party from splitting over the question of Europe before the next election, which must be held by May 1997.
"It's wind and fury and it's certainly irrelevant to the choice which faces the British electorate in the next six months," Health Secretary Stephen Dorrell told the BBC.

Leading Conservatives fear that their electoral chances could be sunk unless the so-called Euro-sceptics, members of parliament fiercely opposed to closer European integration, can somehow be persuaded to keep quiet.

The Conservatives and the opposition Labour party, far ahead in opinion polls, have promised in recent months to hold a referendum on whether or not Britain should enter a European single currency, due to be set up in 1999.
But Goldsmith said on Thursday the single currency was only part of the issue, which was really whether Britons wanted a permanent transfer of sovereignty to European institutions.

The Conservatives are worried that candidates put up by Goldsmith in the general election could siphon off support and hand vital seats to Labour. Goldsmith has promised to dissolve his party once a referendum on Britain's future in Europe takes place.
